# Hip pain

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Pediatric surgery > Hip pain*

[Original Article Link](/library/du0oJ3)

---

## Summary

Hip <u>pain</u> can be a diagnostic challenge due to its diverse etiologies and potential for significant <u>morbidity</u>. It can manifest acutely or gradually and may be traumatic (e.g., <u>fractures</u>, <u>muscle strains</u>, <u>tendon</u> injuries) or atraumatic (e.g., <u>septic arthritis</u>, <u>osteoarthritis</u>). Clinical assessment should include details of the hip <u>pain</u> (e.g., onset, duration, and exacerbating symptoms) and a focused <u>examination of the hip</u>. Most patients presenting with hip <u>pain</u> should be initially evaluated with <u>x-rays</u> of both hip and <u>pelvis</u>, with additional testing based on clinical suspicion. Management is based on the underlying cause.




<u>Lower extremity osteopathy</u> is discussed separately.

---

## Etiology

### Traumatic [[1]](/library/2LdTCq0)[[2]](/library/TLd6Cq0)[[3]](/library/PLdWBq0)[[4]](/library/4Ld3Bq0)




* Bone injury

* <u>Hip fracture</u>

* <u>Acetabular fracture</u>

* Iliac crest <u>apophysis</u> avulsion

* Ischial <u>apophysis</u> avulsion

* <u>Stress fracture</u> (e.g., <u>proximal</u> <u>femur</u>, <u>pelvic</u>)

* <u>Muscle injury</u>

* <u>Avulsion injury</u> (e.g., of gluteal muscle, hamstring)

* Muscle tear (e.g., of gluteal muscle, hamstring)

* <u>Muscle strain</u> (e.g., of hamstring, adductors, <u>obturator internus</u>)

* <u>Obturator internus</u> irritation or strain

* <u>Sports hernia</u>

* <u>Tendon</u> or <u>ligament injury</u>

* Flexor <u>tendon</u> tear or strain

* <u>Proximal</u> hamstring tendinopathy

* <u>Inguinal ligament</u> strain

* <u>Ligamentum teres</u> injury

* <u>Joint</u> injury

* <u>Hip dislocation</u>

* Tear of the <u>acetabular labrum</u>

* <u>Osteochondritis dissecans</u>





### Atraumatic [[1]](/library/2LdTCq0)[[2]](/library/TLd6Cq0)[[3]](/library/PLdWBq0)[[4]](/library/4Ld3Bq0)




* <u>Hip joint</u> pathology

* <u>Avascular necrosis</u>

* <u>Femoroacetabular impingement</u>

* <u>Osteoarthritis</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>

* <u>Septic arthritis</u>

* Chondral lesions or loose bodies

* Ischiofemoral impingement

* <u>Hip joint</u> <u>heterotopic ossification</u>

* Muscle or <u>tendon</u> pathology

* External snapping hip

* <u>Iliopsoas</u> <u>tendinitis</u> or <u>bursitis</u>

* <u>Iliotibial band</u> friction

* <u>Myositis ossificans</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* Gonadal tumors (e.g., <u>ovarian cancer</u>)

* <u>Sarcoma</u>

* <u>Metastasis</u> to the hip [[5]](/library/MLdMyq0)

* <u>Referred pain</u>

* Intra-abdominal (e.g., <u>psoas abscess</u>, inguinal or <u>femoral hernia</u>)

* Intrapelvic (e.g., <u>prostatitis</u>, <u>endometriosis</u>)

* Spinal pathology

* <u>Lumbar spinal stenosis</u>

* <u>Disc herniation</u>

* Disorder of lumbar facets

* <u>Sacroiliac joint</u> dysfunction

* Nerve involvement

* <u>Piriformis syndrome</u>

* <u>Meralgia paresthetica</u>

* Other nerve entrapment (e.g., <u>obturator nerve</u>)

* <u>Pain</u> syndromes

* <u>Greater trochanteric pain syndrome</u>

* <u>Fibromyalgia</u>

* Other

* <u>Claudication</u>

* Inguinal <u>lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Pubic symphysis</u> dysfunction

* <u>Metabolic bone disease</u> (e.g., <u>osteoporosis</u>)





### <u>Hip pain in children</u> [[6]](/library/GqdB-I0)[[7]](/library/tqdXZr0)[[8]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Infectious

* <u>Septic arthritis</u>

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>

* <u>Lyme arthritis</u>

* Inflammatory

* <u>Transient synovitis</u>

* <u>Juvenile idiopathic arthritis</u>

* <u>Reactive arthritis</u>

* <u>IgA vasculitis</u>

* <u>Rheumatic fever</u>

* Trauma and overuse

* <u>Hip fracture</u>

* <u>Hip dislocation</u>

* <u>Muscle strain</u> (e.g., adductor, hip flexors, <u>hamstrings</u>)

* <u>Stress fracture</u> (e.g., femoral neck, pubic rami) [[9]](/library/MqdM_I0)

* <u>Apophysitis</u> (e.g., iliac crest, <u>ischial tuberosity</u>, <u>ASIS</u>) [[10]](/library/iAWJjL0)

* Developmental

* <u>Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease</u> (<u>LCPD</u>)

* <u>Developmental dysplasia of the hip</u> (<u>DDH</u>)

* <u>Slipped capital femoral epiphysis</u> (<u>SCFE</u>)

* <u>Neoplastic</u>

* <u>Osteoid osteoma</u>

* <u>Osteosarcoma</u>

* <u>Ewing sarcoma</u>

* Vascular: <u>Osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>

| <u>Septic arthritis</u> | <br><br>* Any age<br><br>* Acute onset of <u>pain</u> and <u>fever</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u> > 38.5Â°C<br><br>* Child may refuse to bear weight.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* ↑ <u>CRP</u>/<u>ESR</u><br><br>* <u>WBC</u> > 50,000/mmÂ³ on <u>synovial fluid analysis</u><br><br>* Effusion on <u>ultrasound</u><br><br>* Widened <u>joint</u> space on <u>x-ray</u> (but unremarkable in early stages)<br><br>* See “<u>Diagnosis of septic arthritis</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Empiric antibiotics for children with septic arthritis</u><br><br>* Therapeutic <u>arthrocentesis</u><br><br>* Urgent orthopedics consult<br><br>* See “<u>Acute management checklist for septic arthritis</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>SCFE</u> | <br><br>* 10–16 years of age [[25]](/library/rUXfex)<br><br>* Acute on chronic dull <u>pain</u> with <u>antalgic gait</u><br><br>* No <u>fever</u><br><br>* Vague hip and <u>knee pain</u><br><br>* See “<u>Clinical features of SCFE</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>X-ray</u>: displacement of the femoral head<br><br>* See “<u>Diagnosis of SCFE</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Non-weight-bearing</u><br><br>* <u>Pain management in children</u><br><br>* Urgent orthopedics referral for surgical stabilization<br><br>* See “<u>Treatment of SCFE</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>LCPD</u> | <br><br>* 4–10 years of age [[7]](/library/tqdXZr0)<br><br>* Insidious onset<br><br>* No <u>fever</u><br><br>* Vague hip and <u>knee pain</u> (may fluctuate with activity)<br><br>* Can cause the child to limp<br><br>* See “<u>Clinical features of LCPD</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Early <u>x-ray</u> findings: often normal<br><br>* Late <u>x-ray</u> findings: increased lucency of the femoral head and widened <u>joint</u> spaces<br><br>* See “<u>Diagnosis of LCPD</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Conservative therapy</u>: limited <u>weight bearing</u>, <u>physical therapy</u>, bracing<br><br>* <u>Surgery</u> (e.g., <u>femoral osteotomy</u>)<br><br>* See “<u>Treatment of LCPD</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>DDH</u> | <br><br>* Asymptomatic during <u>infancy</u><br><br>* Inability to <u>abduct</u> the hip, hip <u>pain</u>, and limp develop later if uncorrected.<br><br>* See “<u>Clinical features of DDH</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Ultrasound</u> between 4 weeks and 6 months and/or <u>x-ray</u> after 4 months are diagnostic.<br><br>* See “<u>Diagnosis of DDH</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Abduction</u> <u>brace</u> (e.g., <u>Pavlik harness</u>, <u>von Rosen harness</u>)<br><br>* Surgical repair<br><br>* See “<u>Treatment of DDH</u>.”<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Pediatric hip pathologies often present as <u>referred pain</u> in the knee. Children or <u>adolescents</u> presenting with nonspecific <u>knee pain</u> and no findings suggestive of knee pathology require prompt assessment of the hip.
